bibl.title: Engaging in an auditory task suppresses responses in auditory cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how engaging in a task, as distinct from selectively attending, changes sound-evoked responses in auditory cortex
span.quote: To study the neural correlates of one of these non-selective components in auditory cortex, we compared cortical activity elicited by auditory stimuli in animals engaged in an auditory task with activity elicited by identical stimuli when an animal was passive but wakeful; we use the term

span.label: what the neural signature of the non-selective component of attention is in auditory cortex
span.quote: Attention is itself complex, consisting of a well-defined selective component and a much less well-defined component encompassing arousal, vigilance and sustained attention.

span.label: shows task engagement suppresses evoked responses in A1 - the opposite sign to selective attention - and proposes suppression as the wakeful baseline on which other modulations are superimposed
span.quote: We propose that suppression represents the wakeful baseline condition upon which other forms of attentional and non-attentional modulation are superimposed.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Surprisingly, we found that engagement suppressed responses, an effect opposite in sign to that elicited by selective attention.

span.label: task-engagement suppression of sound-evoked responses in auditory cortex
span.quote: To study these preparatory mechanisms, we compared activity in auditory cortex elicited by sounds while rats performed an auditory task (“engaged”) with activity elicited by identical stimuli while subjects were awake but not performing a task (“passive”).

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: After animals reached criterion performance (> 95% correct; ~1 week), we implanted movable tetrodes in the left primary auditory cortex (area A1) to record neural activity, including single unit responses, multi-unit responses and local field potentials (LFPs).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Raised thalamic spontaneous firing depresses thalamocortical synapses, which suppresses the cortical evoked response while leaving cortical spontaneous rate unchanged
span.quote: Synaptic depression of the thalamocortical inputs 15 , 35 could explain how the relative enhancement of the thalamic spontaneous rate in the engaged condition might lead to suppression of the cortical evoked response, without changing the cortical spontaneous activity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Preceding spontaneous activity leaves thalamocortical synapses in a depleted state, so identical thalamic evoked responses drive smaller cortical responses
span.quote: Furthermore, evoked responses of identical magnitude in thalamus would lead to relatively depressed responses in the cortex in the engaged condition, because the thalamocortical synapses would be in a more depleted state due to the preceding spontaneous activity (for details, see SM8: Thalamocortical depression model).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Release probability falls inversely with presynaptic rate, so a higher thalamic firing rate does not translate into a higher cortical spontaneous rate
span.quote: At sufficiently high firing rates, synaptic release probability is inversely proportional to the presynaptic firing rate 36 (P release ∝ 1/F thalamic ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Suppression functions as an early stage of routing the sensory signal to motor centres by silencing neurons irrelevant to the current task
span.quote: Task-engaged suppression may represent an initial stage of this routing, in which activity in neurons irrelevant to the task is reduced.

span.label: thalamic spontaneous rate rises during engagement while thalamic evoked responses do not change
span.quote: In contrast to cortex, there was no difference (p=0.80) in the thalamic evoked response ( Fig. 6a ) between the engaged and passive conditions. However, the thalamic spontaneous activity showed a robust and consistent elevation in the engaged condition

span.label: synaptic depression at thalamocortical synapses could convert a raised thalamic spontaneous rate into a suppressed cortical evoked response without raising cortical spontaneous rate
span.quote: Synaptic depression of the thalamocortical inputs 15 , 35 could explain how the relative enhancement of the thalamic spontaneous rate in the engaged condition might lead to suppression of the cortical evoked response, without changing the cortical spontaneous activity.

span.label: suppression concentrates the same stimulus into fewer, harder-firing neurons - the representation becomes sparser by kurtosis
span.quote: The kurtosis of the firing rate distribution in the engaged condition was greater than in the passive condition (kurtosis engaged = 8.4 ± 2.4 vs. kurtosis passive = 4.1 ± 0.7; p <0.05; see SM5: Kurtosis of firing rate distribution), indicating that the stimulus representation in the engaged condition was sparser.

span.label: headphones deliver identical stimuli regardless of the animal's position, so any difference must come from the animal's state
span.quote: Because the sounds were delivered through headphones, differences in neural activity in this paradigm must be due to differences in the animal’s behavior or state, rather than to differences in the stimulus itself arising from uncontrolled changes in the sound path from speaker to the ear.

span.label: suppression correlates with a cell's spontaneous rate, a property independent of the stimulus used
span.quote: Interestingly, suppression was correlated with spontaneous activity, a property of the cells that does not depend on the stimulus used during the task

span.label: synaptic depression is argued to cover the steady-state effects, with other mechanisms left open for the first few stimuli
span.quote: Thus synaptic depression may account for the steady-state changes in the response to repetitive stimuli, but other mechanisms like feedforward inhibition or axon excitability 43 may play a role during the first few stimuli at high repetition rates

span.label: Simultaneous multi-neuron recording meant stimuli could not be matched to each neuron's receptive field.
span.quote: Because in our experiments we recorded from several neurons simultaneously, we could not optimize the stimulus properties to match the receptive field properties of the recorded neurons.

span.label: The paradigm differs enough from barrel-cortex whisking studies that the two sets of results cannot be compared in detail.
span.quote: However, differences in the behavioral paradigms used in the present work (sensory discrimination tasks modeled after primate studies) and the paradigms used in the barrel system studies (based on active exploration and passive stimulation) preclude a more detailed comparison between these results.

span.label: The attentional load of the task was modest, and a harder task might have reduced or reversed the suppression.
span.quote: The absence of response enhancement to the target stimulus is consistent with the modest attentional load in this task; had the attentional load been greater, the suppression might have been attenuated or even converted into enhancement (assuming that attentional mechanisms are distinct and additive).

span.label: The synaptic and circuit mechanism of the suppression is not established.
span.quote: Our results represent a first step toward understanding the synaptic and circuit mechanisms by which this suppression occurs.

span.label: the absence of target enhancement is attributed to a modest attentional load, so a harder task might have changed the result
span.quote: The absence of response enhancement to the target stimulus is consistent with the modest attentional load in this task; had the attentional load been greater, the suppression might have been attenuated or even converted into enhancement (assuming that attentional mechanisms are distinct and additive).

span.label: a minority of units, 8 of 32, showed the opposite effect
span.quote: Although most single units showed a suppression of evoked activity in the engaged condition, a minority showed an increase (8/32 units). This had the effect of concentrating the stimulus-evoked spikes into smaller population of neurons, each with a relatively higher firing rate.

span.label: suppression interacts with repetition rate and disappears at the highest rates
span.quote: However, at all but the highest repetition rates, the responses in the engaged condition were relatively suppressed relative to the passive condition ( Fig. 2b ). Thus suppression interacts with repetition rate, but is not limited to the initial stimulus.

span.label: the thalamocortical depression account is offered as an explanation that could work, not one that was tested here
span.quote: Synaptic depression of the thalamocortical inputs 15 , 35 could explain how the relative enhancement of the thalamic spontaneous rate in the engaged condition might lead to suppression of the cortical evoked response, without changing the cortical spontaneous activity.

span.label: the two intermodal experiments used a harder task and longer training than the main experiment
span.quote: To increase the difficulty of the task and thereby increase the likelihood of detecting an effect of selective attention 21 , we used a tone discrimination task which was substantially more challenging (~3 weeks training, performance ~ 80%) than the spatial discrimination task (~1 week training, performance >95%) presented above.

span.label: the whisking-versus-quiet suppression in barrel cortex, used as the cross-modal parallel for the same effect
span.quote: Synaptic depression has also been implicated in the barrel cortex, where suppression has been observed during whisking (“engaged”) compared with quiet wakefulness (“passive”), consistent with the present findings

span.label: short-term synaptic depression and the inverse relation between release probability and presynaptic rate, imported as the circuit explanation
span.quote: Synaptic depression of the thalamocortical inputs 15 , 35 could explain how the relative enhancement of the thalamic spontaneous rate in the engaged condition might lead to suppression of the cortical evoked response, without changing the cortical spontaneous activity.

span.label: the tetrodes advanced at least 40 micrometres EVERY DAY
span.quote: We advanced the tetrodes at least 40 μm every day to avoid having multiple recording sessions with the same subset of cells.

span.label: attention is split into a well-defined SELECTIVE component and a much less well-defined non-selective one covering arousal, vigilance and sustained attention - and the two have OPPOSITE signs in this cortex
span.quote: Attention is itself complex, consisting of a well-defined selective component and a much less well-defined component encompassing arousal, vigilance and sustained attention.

span.label: engaged is coined here for the non-selective component: performing a task, as against being awake and not performing one
span.quote: To study the neural correlates of one of these non-selective components in auditory cortex, we compared cortical activity elicited by auditory stimuli in animals engaged in an auditory task with activity elicited by identical stimuli when an animal was passive but wakeful; we use the term

span.label: modulation index is defined twice in this paper with different contents - engaged versus passive in the main experiment, auditory versus olfactory block in the intermodal one
span.quote: In these experiments, we defined the modulation index as: (Activity auditory block − Activity olfactory block )/(Activity auditory block + Activity olfactory block ).

span.label: suppression is proposed not as an effect but as the BASELINE on which other attentional and non-attentional modulations are superimposed
span.quote: We propose that suppression represents the wakeful baseline condition upon which other forms of attentional and non-attentional modulation are superimposed.

span.label: contradicts → prior studies reporting increased spontaneous activity with task engagement (cited as reference 19)
span.quote: 1b–c,e–f,h–i ), in contrast to other studies reporting an increase in spontaneous activity with task engagement 19 .

span.label: builds-on → rat barrel cortex whisking-versus-quiet-wakefulness studies (cited as references 37–39)
span.quote: Suppression in the rat barrel cortex is observed during whisking (“engaged”) compared with quiet wakefulness (“passive”), consistent with the present findings 37 – 39 .

span.label: contradicts → the expectation that engagement, like selective attention, enhances cortical responses
span.quote: We expected that engagement in an auditory task would, like selective attention, lead to an enhancement of stimulus-evoked responses in the auditory cortex 8 , 16 – 19 . Surprisingly, we found just the opposite: in the engaged condition, neural responses to all components of the stimulus — both target and non-target — were consistently suppressed.

span.label: contradicts → the account of neural activity as a resource allocated in greater measure with increasing arousal
span.quote: These results demonstrate that in auditory cortex, neural activity cannot be viewed simply as a limited resource allocated in greater measure as the state of the animal passes from somnolent to passively listening to engaged and attentive. Instead the engaged condition possesses a characteristic and distinct neural signature in which sound-evoked responses are paradoxically suppressed.

span.label: qualifies → studies reporting increased spontaneous activity with task engagement
span.quote: This suppression of evoked responses was not accompanied by any change in the spontaneous activity preceding stimulus presentation ( Fig. 1b–c,e–f,h–i ), in contrast to other studies reporting an increase in spontaneous activity with task engagement

span.label: supports → barrel cortex reports of suppression during whisking relative to quiet wakefulness
span.quote: Synaptic depression has also been implicated in the barrel cortex, where suppression has been observed during whisking (“engaged”) compared with quiet wakefulness (“passive”), consistent with the present findings

span.label: distinguishes-from → sleep and anaesthesia, which have their own distinct signatures
span.quote: Spontaneous and evoked cortical activity showed a characteristic neural signature under each condition ( Table T1 ): spontaneous cortical activity was reduced in the less aroused states (sleep and anesthetized) compared with the awake but passive condition. The distinct neural signatures associated with sleep and anesthesia indicate that these states are different from the passive but wakeful condition.

span.label: engaged —distinct-from→ selective attention
span.note: OPPOSITE IN SIGN in the same cortex - the sharpest sign contrast in the corpus, and the reason the construct has to be split
span.quote: Surprisingly, we found that engagement suppressed responses, an effect opposite in sign to that elicited by selective attention.

span.label: engaged —causes→ auditory cortex
span.note: suppresses evoked responses; SCOPE: not at the highest repetition rates, and 8 of 32 units go the other way
span.quote: Suppression of the evoked response was observed for most of the responsive (SM2: Stimulus response analysis) single units ( Fig. 1e , p<0.01). Suppression was also observed for measures of neural population activity, including multiunit activity ( Fig. 1f , p<1e–16) and evoked LFP ( Fig. 1g , p<1e

span.label: RETRACTED (THE SPAN IS A NULL RESULT AND THE EDGE IS CAUSAL) · engaged —causes→ auditory thalamus
span.note: RETRACTED: THE SPAN IS A NULL RESULT AND THE EDGE IS CAUSAL. `engaged --causes--> auditory thalamus` stands on 'In contrast to cortex, THERE WAS NO DIFFERENCE (p=0.80) in the thalamic evoked response'. The sentence reports that engagement did NOT change the thalamic response - it is the control that makes the cortical effect interpretable, and it is the paper's point that the thalamus is where the effect is ABSENT. Recorded as the effect being present. Same shape as the sameness-under-a-difference-edge family, arriving through `causes` instead. — raises SPONTANEOUS rate only, leaving evoked responses unchanged - opposite structure to the cortical effect
span.quote: In contrast to cortex, there was no difference (p=0.80) in the thalamic evoked response ( Fig. 6a ) between the engaged and passive conditions. However, the thalamic spontaneous activity showed a robust and consistent elevation in the engaged condition

span.label: synaptic depression —causes→ auditory cortex
span.note: could explain - proposed, not tested here
span.quote: Synaptic depression of the thalamocortical inputs 15 , 35 could explain how the relative enhancement of the thalamic spontaneous rate in the engaged condition might lead to suppression of the cortical evoked response, without changing the cortical spontaneous activity.

span.label: engaged —distinct-from→ arousal
span.note: argued from the SIGN: raised arousal would raise firing, and firing fell
span.quote: However, this did not seem likely to explain the suppression we observed, since the increase in arousal in the engaged condition would have been expected to increase cortical excitability and thereby increase evoked or spontaneous firing rates 2 , 3 , 19 , effects opposite in sign from those we observed.

span.label: engaged —operationalised-as→ kurtosis
span.note: the sparsening consequence, measured rather than the state itself
span.quote: The kurtosis of the firing rate distribution in the engaged condition was greater than in the passive condition (kurtosis engaged = 8.4 ± 2.4 vs. kurtosis passive = 4.1 ± 0.7; p <0.05; see SM5: Kurtosis of firing rate distribution), indicating that the stimulus representation in the engaged condition was sparser.

span.label: paired t-test
span.quote: Rather, the suppression of the responses to the target stimulus was indistinguishable ( Fig. 2d–e and Fig. S2c : Single unit responses to task relevant and task irrelevant stimuli are equally suppressed during the task) from that of the last non-target stimulus in the stimulus train (paired t-test, p>0.1).

span.label: kurtosis
span.quote: The kurtosis of the firing rate distribution in the engaged condition was greater than in the passive condition (kurtosis engaged = 8.4 ± 2.4 vs. kurtosis passive = 4.1 ± 0.7; p <0.05; see SM5: Kurtosis of firing rate distribution), indicating that the stimulus representation in the engaged condition was sparser.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Subjects performed a trial every 9.03±0.16 sec (mean±s.e.m) for ~200 trials per recording session.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Interestingly, suppression was correlated with spontaneous activity, a property of the cells that does not depend on the stimulus used during the task (see Fig. S4 : Cortical units with high spontaneous firing rates show less suppression of the evoked response during the task).

span.label: p-value
span.quote: Suppression was also observed for measures of neural population activity, including multiunit activity ( Fig. 1f , p<1e–16) and evoked LFP ( Fig. 1g , p<1e–16).

span.label: Mahalanobis distance (spike-cluster quality metric)
span.quote: The ID is defined as the Mahalanobis distance from the center of an identified cluster within which as many spikes belong to the specified cluster as others.

span.label: modulation index
span.quote: We quantified these effects across the population with a modulation index, defined as: (Activity engaged − Activity passive )/(Activity engaged + Activity passive ). The modulation index ranges from −1 (complete suppression in the engaged condition) to +1 (complete suppression in the passive condition)

span.label: kurtosis of the firing rate distribution
span.term: kurtosis of the firing rate distribution
span.quote: The kurtosis of the firing rate distribution in the engaged condition was greater than in the passive condition (kurtosis engaged = 8.4 ± 2.4 vs. kurtosis passive = 4.1 ± 0.7; p <0.05; see SM5: Kurtosis of firing rate distribution), indicating that the stimulus representation in the engaged condition was sparser.

span.label: paired t-test
span.quote: However, the response to the target stimulus was not enhanced ( Fig. 2c ; see also Fig. S2a–b : Single unit responses to task relevant and task irrelevant stimuli are equally suppressed during the task). Rather, the suppression of the responses to the target stimulus was indistinguishable ( Fig. 2d–e and Fig. S2c : Single unit responses to task relevant and task irrelevant stimuli are equally suppressed during the task) from that of the last non-target stimulus in the stimulus train (paired t-test, p>0.1).

span.label: Engaging in an auditory task suppressed sound-evoked responses in auditory cortex, the opposite sign of the enhancement produced by selective attention.
span.quote: Surprisingly, we found that engagement suppressed responses, an effect opposite in sign to that elicited by selective attention.

span.label: The suppression of evoked responses occurred with no accompanying change in pre-stimulus spontaneous cortical activity.
span.quote: This suppression of evoked responses was not accompanied by any change in the spontaneous activity preceding stimulus presentation ( Fig. 1b–c,e–f,h–i ), in contrast to other studies reporting an increase in spontaneous activity with task engagement 19 .

span.label: Responses to the task-relevant target sound were suppressed just as much as responses to the irrelevant non-target sound, so the effect is not selective withdrawal of attention from non-targets.
span.quote: Rather, the suppression of the responses to the target stimulus was indistinguishable ( Fig. 2d–e and Fig. S2c : Single unit responses to task relevant and task irrelevant stimuli are equally suppressed during the task) from that of the last non-target stimulus in the stimulus train (paired t-test, p>0.1).

span.label: Sound-evoked responses during auditory-attention blocks were not suppressed relative to olfactory-attention blocks, showing the suppression follows task engagement rather than the auditory modality of the task.
span.quote: There was no net suppression of sound-evoked responses elicited during the auditory block compared with those elicited during the olfactory block ( Fig. 3a–b ).

span.label: The amount of suppression was unrelated to a neuron's spatial selectivity, frequency selectivity, or the octave distance between its best frequency and the attended frequency.
span.quote: However, there was no correlation between the modulation index and spatial selectivity ( Fig. 2f and Fig. S2d : Single unit responses to task relevant and task irrelevant stimuli are equally suppressed during the task), frequency selectivity ( Fig. 3e ), or the distance in octaves between the best frequency and the attended frequency ( Fig. 3f and Fig. S3 : Measurement of cortical tuning curves).

span.label: Suppression persisted in a head-fixed task in which the stimulus started randomly rather than being triggered by the animal, ruling out self-triggering as the cause.
span.quote: We therefore conclude that the suppression observed in the engaged condition does not depend on the animal triggering the stimulus.

span.label: Because a minority of neurons increased their firing while most were suppressed, the engaged-state representation was sparser, with kurtosis rising from 4.1 to 8.4.
span.quote: The kurtosis of the firing rate distribution in the engaged condition was greater than in the passive condition (kurtosis engaged = 8.4 ± 2.4 vs. kurtosis passive = 4.1 ± 0.7; p <0.05; see SM5: Kurtosis of firing rate distribution), indicating that the stimulus representation in the engaged condition was sparser.

span.label: In the auditory thalamus engagement left evoked responses unchanged but raised spontaneous firing rates, the opposite pattern to cortex.
span.quote: In the auditory thalamus, however, engagement enhanced spontaneous firing rates but did not affect evoked responses.

span.label: Thalamic evoked responses were statistically identical between engaged and passive conditions (p=0.80).
span.quote: In contrast to cortex, there was no difference (p=0.80) in the thalamic evoked response ( Fig. 6a ) between the engaged and passive conditions.

span.label: Sleep and ketamine anesthesia reduced spontaneous cortical activity relative to the awake passive state, giving those low-arousal states a neural signature distinct from passive wakefulness.
span.quote: Spontaneous and evoked cortical activity showed a characteristic neural signature under each condition ( Table T1 ): spontaneous cortical activity was reduced in the less aroused states (sleep and anesthetized) compared with the awake but passive condition.

span.label: Neural activity did not differ between the passive blocks recorded before and after the task, excluding recording drift, satiety and reward expectation as explanations for the suppression.
span.quote: There was no change (p>0.2) in neural activity between the first and second passive block of trials (i.e. between the passive block before and after the engaged block), indicating that suppression was not due to nonstationarities in the recording, satiety, reward expectation, arousal, etc. (see SM4: Comparison of neural activity between first and second passive block).

span.label: task engagement suppressed evoked responses across single units, multiunit activity and LFP
span.quote: Suppression of the evoked response was observed for most of the responsive (SM2: Stimulus response analysis) single units ( Fig. 1e , p<0.01). Suppression was also observed for measures of neural population activity, including multiunit activity ( Fig. 1f , p<1e–16) and evoked LFP ( Fig. 1g , p<1e

span.label: cortical spontaneous activity did not change, unlike other reports
span.quote: This suppression of evoked responses was not accompanied by any change in the spontaneous activity preceding stimulus presentation ( Fig. 1b–c,e–f,h–i ), in contrast to other studies reporting an increase in spontaneous activity with task engagement

span.label: task-relevant target and irrelevant non-target stimuli were suppressed equally
span.quote: However, the response to the target stimulus was not enhanced ( Fig. 2c ; see also Fig. S2a–b : Single unit responses to task relevant and task irrelevant stimuli are equally suppressed during the task). Rather, the suppression of the responses to the target stimulus was indistinguishable ( Fig. 2d–e and Fig. S2c : Single unit responses to task relevant and task irrelevant stimuli are equally suppressed during the task) from that of the last non-target stimulus in the stimulus train (paired t-test, p>0.1).

span.label: the representation became sparser, kurtosis 8.4 engaged against 4.1 passive
span.quote: The kurtosis of the firing rate distribution in the engaged condition was greater than in the passive condition (kurtosis engaged = 8.4 ± 2.4 vs. kurtosis passive = 4.1 ± 0.7; p <0.05; see SM5: Kurtosis of firing rate distribution), indicating that the stimulus representation in the engaged condition was sparser.

span.label: no suppression of auditory responses in an auditory block relative to an olfactory block
span.quote: These results are inconsistent with the hypothesis that engaging in an auditory task per se suppresses responses in auditory cortex, and support the interpretation advanced above that suppression results from engaging in a task, regardless of sensory modality.

span.label: suppression appeared in both blocks relative to passive, so it does not depend on the task's modality
span.quote: As a further test, we compared responses in all three conditions (passive, engaged-auditory, engaged-olfactory) in a single animal performing another intermodal attention task (see Methods: Task 3). As expected, sound-evoked responses were suppressed in both the auditory and the olfactory blocks compared with the passive block, and responses during the auditory block were not suppressed relative to the responses during the olfactory block ( Fig. 3c–d ). Thus, engaging in an auditory task did not elicit a reduction in acoustically-evoked responses relative to engaging in an olfactory task, in marked contrast to the robust suppression of acoustically-evoked responses relative to the passive condition. We therefore conclude that the general suppression observed in the purely auditory task did not depend on the auditory nature of the task.

span.label: suppression was unrelated to spatial selectivity, frequency selectivity or distance from the attended frequency
span.quote: This raised the possibility that the suppression we observed in the engaged condition was due to attentional suppression in the majority of neurons which were stimulated suboptimally. To test this hypothesis, we recorded tuning curves and assessed the relationship between the receptive field and the modulation index of the evoked responses. We expected that if suppression arose from the presentation of suboptimal stimuli, then the modulation index should increase with stimulus selectivity or with the degree to which the best frequency matched the attended frequency. However, there was no correlation between the modulation index and spatial selectivity ( Fig. 2f and Fig. S2d : Single unit responses to task relevant and task irrelevant stimuli are equally suppressed during the task), frequency selectivity ( Fig. 3e ), or the distance in octaves between the best frequency and the attended frequency ( Fig. 3f and Fig. S3 : Measurement of cortical tuning curves). Interestingly, suppression was correlated with spontaneous activity, a property of the cells that does not depend on the stimulus used during the task (see Fig. S4 : Cortical units with high spontaneous firing rates show less suppression of the evoked response during the task). Thus in summary, task-engaged suppression cannot be readily predicted from receptive field properties.

span.label: the same suppression appeared when the animal did not trigger the stimulus, with a nearly identical modulation index
span.quote: The modulation index of the evoked responses for multiunit activity was −0.20 ± 0.03, which was very similar to the values obtained in the task in Fig. 1 , −0.19±0.02.

span.label: sleep and anaesthesia have their own distinct signatures, with reduced spontaneous activity
span.quote: Spontaneous and evoked cortical activity showed a characteristic neural signature under each condition ( Table T1 ): spontaneous cortical activity was reduced in the less aroused states (sleep and anesthetized) compared with the awake but passive condition. The distinct neural signatures associated with sleep and anesthesia indicate that these states are different from the passive but wakeful condition.

span.label: in thalamus, spontaneous activity rose during engagement while evoked responses were unchanged
span.quote: In contrast to cortex, there was no difference (p=0.80) in the thalamic evoked response ( Fig. 6a ) between the engaged and passive conditions. However, the thalamic spontaneous activity showed a robust and consistent elevation in the engaged condition

span.label: thalamic burstiness did not change, unlike in sleep or reduced arousal
span.quote: No changes were observed in the burstiness of the thalamic cells (SM7: Bursts in thalamus), in contrast to elevated burstiness associated with sleep or reduced arousal

span.quote: To study the neural correlates of one of these non-selective components in auditory cortex, we compared cortical activity elicited by auditory stimuli in animals engaged in an auditory task with activity elicited by identical stimuli when an animal was passive but wakeful; we use the term “engaged” to refer to this non-selective component.

span.quote: The non-target stimulus consisted of a train of clicks (5 msec white noise bursts; repetition rate from 2–35 Hz, a range over which cortical responses show strong modulation 14 , 15 ) presented diotically for 1.8 seconds, beginning after a variable (400–600 msec) period following trial initiation.

span.quote: Interestingly, suppression was correlated with spontaneous activity, a property of the cells that does not depend on the stimulus used during the task

span.label: −0.20 ± 0.03 vs −0.19±0.02 — modulation index of the multiunit evoked response in the head-fixed task compared with the freely moving task
span.quote: The modulation index of the evoked responses for multiunit activity was −0.20 ± 0.03, which was very similar to the values obtained in the task in Fig. 1 , −0.19±0.02.

span.label: 8.4 ± 2.4 vs 4.1 ± 0.7 — kurtosis of the firing-rate distribution when engaged versus passive
span.quote: The kurtosis of the firing rate distribution in the engaged condition was greater than in the passive condition (kurtosis engaged = 8.4 ± 2.4 vs. kurtosis passive = 4.1 ± 0.7; p <0.05; see SM5: Kurtosis of firing rate distribution), indicating that the stimulus representation in the engaged condition was sparser.

span.label: 8/32 units — minority of single units whose evoked activity increased rather than decreased when the animal was engaged
span.quote: Although most single units showed a suppression of evoked activity in the engaged condition, a minority showed an increase (8/32 units).

span.label: p<1e–16 — significance of the engagement-related suppression for multiunit activity and evoked LFP
span.quote: Suppression was also observed for measures of neural population activity, including multiunit activity ( Fig. 1f , p<1e–16) and evoked LFP ( Fig. 1g , p<1e–16).

span.label: p=0.80 — test of the difference in thalamic evoked response between engaged and passive conditions (no difference)
span.quote: In contrast to cortex, there was no difference (p=0.80) in the thalamic evoked response ( Fig. 6a ) between the engaged and passive conditions.

span.label: p<0.001 — significance of the elevation of thalamic spontaneous activity during engagement
span.quote: However, the thalamic spontaneous activity showed a robust and consistent elevation in the engaged condition ( Fig. 6b–c ; p<0.001).

span.label: 81% / 91% — behavioural accuracy during auditory versus olfactory blocks of the intermodal attention task
span.quote: Performance was 81% during the auditory blocks and 91% during the olfactory blocks, indicating that the subjects understood the block structures of the task.

span.label: > 95% correct; ~1 week — criterion performance and training time on the two-alternative choice task before electrode implantation
span.quote: After animals reached criterion performance (> 95% correct; ~1 week), we implanted movable tetrodes in the left primary auditory cortex (area A1) to record neural activity, including single unit responses, multi-unit responses and local field potentials (LFPs).

span.label: kurtosis 8.4 plus or minus 2.4 engaged versus 4.1 plus or minus 0.7 passive — sparseness of the representation
span.quote: The kurtosis of the firing rate distribution in the engaged condition was greater than in the passive condition (kurtosis engaged = 8.4 ± 2.4 vs. kurtosis passive = 4.1 ± 0.7; p <0.05; see SM5: Kurtosis of firing rate distribution), indicating that the stimulus representation in the engaged condition was sparser.

span.label: 8 of 32 units — the minority showing enhancement rather than suppression
span.quote: Although most single units showed a suppression of evoked activity in the engaged condition, a minority showed an increase (8/32 units). This had the effect of concentrating the stimulus-evoked spikes into smaller population of neurons, each with a relatively higher firing rate.

span.label: about 80% correct after three weeks versus over 95% after one week — the harder intermodal task against the main task
span.quote: To increase the difficulty of the task and thereby increase the likelihood of detecting an effect of selective attention 21 , we used a tone discrimination task which was substantially more challenging (~3 weeks training, performance ~ 80%) than the spatial discrimination task (~1 week training, performance >95%) presented above.
